utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We're back to business as usual after, almost, one month of vacation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution. I appear here, with Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution. I would also like to inform Your Honours that Mr. Niemann is scheduled to be in a number of different courtrooms in the next two weeks, so he has asked for Your Honours' indulgence for not being here. He will be here at various times. Because he's not here, we also have Mr. Jim Cowles for the Prosecution who will be assisting us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the defence presentation, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. I hope Your Honours, the information we just received from my learned colleague, Ms. McHenry, is not going to affect the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination of the witnesses which we have just called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Zelko Olujic, an attorney from Croatia. I would like to introduce Tomislav Kuzmanovic, an attorney from the US, who along with me today is also representing Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic. I'm defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic along with my colleague Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm counsel for Esad Landzo. Ms. McMurrey is not here this morning. She is still in the States attending a funeral and perhaps I can tell you tomorrow when she'll be back. I haven't spoken to her, having just flown in from Sarajevo and Vienna this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your great effort in getting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The LiveNote computers are not working for Mr. Moran and myself. Perhaps someone can check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you see if they can get the computers to work, please? We have observed that counsel has not completely complied with the order we made as to submission of witnesses and the evidence they are likely to give. Apart from this one, I know counsel, for second accused, I'm not sure I received anything from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Delic, we had a miscommunication between Sarajevo and Houston. It just didn't get done and we are going to do it tonight. I will file it with a motion and request to file late, and I have already talked to the Prosecution about it and it will be an unopposed motion. My apologies to the court. Frankly, e-mail between Sarajevo and Houston was just -- we had a miscommunication and I'll take full responsibility for it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that on the 15th, we have furnished a complete list in compliance with your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My attention has just been turned to it. Mr. Olujic, you have not submitted a list with your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we sent a witness list and we had provided it within the time frame that was provided by you on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have not been given a summary of their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the list I see here supposed to mean that these are the witnesses you intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at this point, yes. That is the witness list, which the defence of Mr. Zdravko Mucic is providing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was to be a summary of the evidence of each witness, separately. That was the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our submission, we have provided what we understood the essence of the witness's testimony is going to be. However, if it is necessary for us to provide a summary of each individual witness's testimony, that may end up being an entire volume. Now, if the Trial Chamber so insists, we will provide that, but from our submission, we have given the overview of witnesses in terms of those who were qualified witnesses and those who were kept and detained in the Celebici collection centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber assumed you were dealing with counsel, that is what we assumed, who are trying these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have given such a long list, the impression is it is an attempt to separatise the whole trial. Therefore, we want to be satisfied that the witnesses you mentioned are really relevant, so please supply us with a summary of the evidence of each witness separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Anybody who you remember was passing by could be a witness or the whole city could be witnesses. That's why we thought we were dealing with counsel who are involved in this case and who understand the case they are dealing with and who know the accusations against the accused persons and who have offences against them, not those who are playing. We are not here for a joke, you know. These are very serious matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours, but my client is responsible for certain actions that are based on the indictment, and if the Prosecution has offered a number of witnesses but may have also interviewed an additional number of witnesses which may have had exculpatory statements regarding my client, then we reserve the right to bring any witness who can shed some light. I don't know whether this is going to be 5, 10, 50 witnesses. We do not know at this stage, but we believe that all these witnesses are relevant to the very charge of the objective responsibilities. So the Prosecution has brought on dozens of witnesses and they have also interviewed hundreds of witnesses. If they were given freedom to go about their case in a way they saw fit, then we do not feel that 99 witnesses, which may all, to some extent, be relevant or speak to the facts of the case be brought here. We believe, and our client believes, that it would not be out of place to call this many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In view of such a large list, we want to be sure they are relevant. In order to save time at the Tribunal and the expense, you must write us with a summary of the evidence of each witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This looks very much like a nuisance. This is not a list of witnesses. How far have you gone with getting the computers working? Is it working now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technical people have told me we're going to have to wait until the break. I can live with that. If it's okay with Mr. O'Sullivan, it's okay with me. I remember how to take notes. I still know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you can bear with us for the short period?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: This is new for me speaking into a mic. I noticed that in my translation, large hunks of what I said was not there. Perhaps it was because I didn't have the microphone on, although Cynthia had warned me that I must do better with my Texas accent or no one will be able to understand me. Let me just say that the only information I have -- I understand that Cynthia McMurrey has submitted something to the court in response. Just this morning, the taxi driver gave me a fax that came to the hotel from Cynthia saying that she would try to call me last night, but obviously we weren't able to get out of Sarajevo and did not arrive until this morning. So if I can ask the court for another day, I will speak to her tonight and hopefully be able to respond better in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we might as well continue with the cross-examination of our last witness. Ms. Residovic, I think we are still on your last witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is Mr. Enver Tahirovic, and his testimony is to be continued, his cross-examination, actually. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat. Mr. Olujic, I believe you are cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No questions from us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have some questions. ENVER TAHIROVIC Cross-examined by Ms. McHenry

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, my name is Teresa McHenry. I'm going to be asking you some questions. If you don't understand my question, please just tell me and I will repeat or rephrase it. Sir, you testified that -- can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually, even a bit too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that in April of 1992, you were senior advisor for All People's Defence in the health centre in Konjic and that you held that position until the 18th of May. When did you first become senior advisor for All People's Defence in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand me correct. I finished the studies of All People's Defence in Konjic and this kind of education existed only in the former Yugoslavia. There was a faculty, a school for All People's Defence, and I became a professor. After I graduated in 1980, I got a job at the health centre in Konjic where I was an advisor for the All People's Defence, that is, I was to consult the health centre on the issues of All People's Defence in case of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that position a military position, a civilian position or did it have elements of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a military school, military academy. I was a civilian throughout this time, but I finished this kind of school, and it was -- it only existed in the former Yugoslavia. Every institution, every company in the former Yugoslavia had to have a person of that education that was to be in compliance with the Marxist theory of the armed population. So most of the institutions in the former Yugoslavia had a unit or some kind of a group that worked on the issues of defence. But throughout this period, I was a civilian. I was not a military person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of the All People's Defence, until 18th of May, were you considered part of the TO, in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the day the mobilisation was called in my country, I put myself at the disposal of the TO staff, but right away they said that I should stay in the health centre so we could complete the preparations so that the health centre would be prepared, that it would be ready to receive the injured, the sick, and I stayed there until 18 May, and so I was involved in the defence of my country in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After you took a position with the TO staff on the 18th of May, did you have any duties as part of the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I moved to the TO staff, that is the joint command at that time, I became an officer in the operations body. And this is a body which really was involved in preparations for combat actions and on the basis of these preparations, a proposal would be sent to the commander on what to do. But I believe that this was all within the All People's Defence scope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, within the TO staff, what exact positions did you hold between the 18th of May and your appointment as head of municipal headquarters in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the TO staff, I was an officer in the operations body. Then, sometime in October, I was appointed chief of staff and we're talking about 1992. In the middle of 1993, I was appointed commander of the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, during the Oganj operation, you would agree with me that you function as commander of town security, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more like officer on duty at the staff. In the statement that I gave to the Defence, I already said that at that time, in the territory of Konjic municipality, there were already certain misunderstandings with the HVO, so somebody had to stay behind and take care of things. We still had defence lines against the Serbs, and so somebody would have to ensure, and I'm not sure how much you have a picture of where we were, we were attacking from sort of this side over here and under here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, with respect to a number of questions, it may be that the answer need only be yes or no, and so sometimes we don't need detailed explanations. So is it correct that whatever your official title was, in effect, what you were functioning as was commander of town security?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. The witness said that he was an officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what counsel was asking was his specific duty was. I think if he knows what his specific duty was at that time, he should be able to say it. His duty, but what was his specific duty, this is what counsel was asking, and I don't see the need for objecting to him telling the Tribunal what his specific duty was. I hope I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. I heard the counsel's question asking whether he was a commander of the town, and this is the only thing that I reacted to, but I take your comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe the witness had answered the question, but the answer was not translated. If the translators remember, if they could give us the answer, otherwise I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it also the case that later on you had command of military units while you were in the TO staff, before you were appointed chief in January of 1993, before that time, at various occasions, you had command of military units, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a period in July when I was at Mount Tisavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't really need an explanation, just confirm it with a yes, that's a fair answer, I don't need you to explain it. And I fact, I think we'll get through it quicker. There may be some things that I'll ask you to explain, but otherwise, if you can just answer yes or no fairly, that's fine. Now, sir, you stated in May that you were offered a job as commander of Celebici and you turned it down. Starting with the later part of May and going until the time the Celebici camp for Serb prisoners closed, who was the commander of Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know exactly. Perhaps, sometime around the end of August when it was the OECD, we called it the camps. When I went there, I think I saw Mr. Zdravko Mucic there. I think this was the end of August, beginning of September. Because prior to that period there was combat all the time, so that I didn't go there often, I went there very rarely to the Celebici prison. The part where the ammunition, food and equipment was stored for our units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that, prior to the end of August, you do not know who the commander of Celebici camp was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just want to confirm there is no--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I didn't know before that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned previously a statement you gave to the Defence. You would agree that in the prior statement to the Defence you stated and I quote, "I know that Zdravko Mucic, called Pavo, was appointed to the post of prison commander late in May or in the beginning of June? You would agree with me that you have previously said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please read it? Could you please read exactly what I said word by word?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that Zdravko Mucic called Pavo was appointed to the post of the prison commander late in May or in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I also said that I saw commander Omer Boric decision saying that I was appointed deputy and Mucic commander of the Celebici barracks. That is what should be stated there. So I don't know whether Pavo was appointed. I saw a draft in handwriting of an order -- I saw this order being prepared. The order, according to which Pavo Mucic was to be appointed commander of the Celebici barracks and me as deputy. I rejected that and I remained in the operations department. Whether Mr. Mucic was, in fact, appointed commander at that time, I really do not know. On June the 2nd I went to visit my family on the seaside on the island of Korcula. And when I came back the commander was Esad Ramic. So I never saw an order or read an order whereby Pavo Mucic was appointed commander. I'm sorry, not Pavo, Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to verify, when you say that you came back from visiting your family on the seaside and Mr. Ramic was commander, you mean Mr. Ramic was commander of the TO, not of Celebici barracks, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you presenting at the meeting where Mr. Delalic proposed that Mr. Mucic be commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic have a close personal relationship before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic a part of the TO, the HVO, the MUP, the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see Mr. Mucic in uniform, but I don't know whether he belonged to the TO or the HVO because the uniforms were the same and we didn't have insignia on our sleeves. I may have seen him two or three times at the joint command, not after that. As I told you, the first time I went to the prison, the area where the prisoners were kept in detention, that is when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Mucic in August of 1992, do you know at that point if he was a member of the TO, HVO or some other body or none of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and Major Kevric, now colonel, were sent there with this team that wanted to visit the prison. And at the entrance to the prison, we were met by Mr. Hazim Delic and Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Our visit had been announced by telephone so that I really don't know at that moment whether he was representing the HVO or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you testified that in May of 1992, Mr. Ramic was placed in a room in the health centre because of his heart problem and because he needed quiet, when exactly was this as best you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is that really relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe some limited discussion of the 40 in Konjic at this time and how there was -- this is relevant. Because we believe it's relevant how Mr. Delalic was able to get authority in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Authority over what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Authority over Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that Mr. Ramic was placed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the date, but I think it was a day or two before I joined the joint command, so it must have been the 16th or the 17th of May. I assumed that was the date because I spent, perhaps, one day with him in that room where we stayed and then I went to the meeting of the joint command and did not come back to the Konjic's Hospital to work there, but rather I stayed in the joint command building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Ramic performed any duties for the TO during the period he was in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a meeting we held, after the meeting at which the joint command was formerly established, he was appointed to the post of assistant chief of department for operative and educational affairs. He was my immediate superior. But for a time he did not perform his duties because he was sick and the commander was Ahmed Boric at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have testified that you were present during the meeting on the 18th of May between the war presidency and the Defence forces and you've also testified that it was on that date that you and Mr. Delalic were appointed. My question is, did you ever, yourself, see Mr. Delalic's formal appointment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think this is a fair question. I think the witness never said that at that meeting, Delalic was appointed as anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let me go back. Let me just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Delalic's appointment at any time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His appointment for what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: His appointment as coordinator, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the actual document, the paper on which it was stated?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I had just heard that he had been appointed coordinator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a few days after Mr. Delalic's appointment, did you and Mr. Delalic's and some other people have a meeting in Mr. Delalic's house where he informed you about his appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was any such meeting, I didn't attend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to the meeting of the 18th of May, you would agree with me that a reason for the meeting on the 18th of May was to discuss the need for the organisation of the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you repeat it, please, something must be wrong with the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, sir, that a reason for the meeting on the 18th of May, was to discuss the need for the organisation of the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how you will understand what I am going to say. It was a meeting that was to deal with a certain number of problems regarding the competencies of individual people. What were the competencies of the military bodies and what of the civilian ones. Who should ensure food supplies, who should bury the dead, who should take care of other civilian affairs and who should defend the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you more specifically. You would agree with me that a reason for Mr. Delalic's appointment as coordinator was to settle the disputes that had been occurring between the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the time. At that time, the relations were very good and correct. There was no conflict between the TO and the HVO at that time because we had just formed the joint command and filled in the vacancies after its formation a couple of days before. There was no conflict between the TO and the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, wouldn't you agree with me, that in a prior statement, you talked about the disputes between the HVO and the TO and you then went on to say in order to settle those disputes, the war presidency of the Konjic municipalities, appointed Zejnil Delalic to the post of coordinator among the war presidency, the HVO, the TO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between the war presidency and the military structures, but not between the HVO and the TO. So between the military bodies and the civilian bodies and the link between the two, between the military and the civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then read to you the paragraph beforehand, which refers to those disputes. And tell me if this is what you have previously have stated, "This body, the joint command, were supposed to have the following chain of command: Esad Ramic was superior to us, the operation officers, whereas Dinko Zebic and Omer Boric were superior to him. Thus, the HVO units would not be subordinated to the authorities in Grude. However, it soon became obvious, in everyday life --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO was obeying only their own chain of command and disputes began to arise. In order to settle those disputes, the war presidency of the Konjic municipality appointed Zejnil Delalic to the post of coordinator. Is that what you previously have stated, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know whether that is exactly what it says in my statement and whether I said that, maybe the lady taking the statement put it down by mistake, but I don't know that Zejnil Delalic was acting to prevent any misunderstandings between the HVO and the TO. As far as I know, he didn't even attend every meeting. He attended a couple when problems were discussed, logistical problems, because you must see, we were an army in the process of being formed. We had no warehouses of our own, no equipment, no ammunition. And the roll of logistics was taken over by the civilian authorities because that is their duty according to the Constitution. And a link was needed between them and us as the military structure, so that everything should function as well as possible. And that is the post of coordinator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Mr. Delalic stated that one of his functions was to resolve disputes between the HVO and the TO; that would be different than our understanding of his functions, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what Mr. Delalic said, but my understanding of the roll of coordinator and what I saw at the time had to do with what I have just said because there were no real conflicts. There were misunderstandings. There are disagreements in amongst us even. We are different people and disagreements arise. But the HVO was directly subordinated to the headquarters in Grude. We had an inferior position in relation to our main headquarters and the MUP had its chain of command leading to the republican MUP. And all of us together were turned towards our war presidency at the time and we needed a link to combine all this together to make sure that the defensive preparations are done properly and that we are able to accomplish our task and that is the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going back for a moment to the minutes to the 18th of May meeting, the minutes of that meeting state that all commanders must have exactly established lists of their units and that all members of the military should be clearly marked by signs on their uniforms. Was this conclusion implemented and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the marks are concerned for members of the TO, throughout the war -- we were not able to carry out before the end -- before 1995 because we didn't have a chance to produce proper insignia. Some people had some, some others, but the army was not properly formed and structured and marked. Even now, you can see members of the army, of the federation, without insignia because this is an army in the process of formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just a minute ago and also during your direct, you sometimes refer to the official or the legal position. Now, sir, you would agree with me that at least on some occasions, the legal or official position was not the position in fact in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I am really not a jurist and I don't really understand what you want to ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just ask you more specific, you would agree with me that the HVO was not legalised as an official component of the armed forces of Bosnia, but it was treated as such during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the middle of May. As of mid-May, it officially became a component part of the defence forces, so that our name was the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this included both the HVO and the army. So at the very beginning of the war, because of their wish to join in the defence of the country, they were legalised by us, in Konjic, and as of mid-May, they were formerly legalised by law as part of the defence forces of our country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they were part of the defence forces of the country, did they report to the same chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They never officially recognised our supreme command. Their command, throughout the war, was in Grude and in Mostar, that is Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me, that officially, according to the set-up of the joint command, the head of the TO were supposed to be superior to all the HVO soldiers, but that was not the reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe there's a mistake in the translation, I got T V O -- I'm sorry, could you please repeat the question, I didn't quite get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that after the joint command was officially set up, Mr. Ramic was supposed to be officially, the head of all the troops in Konjic, including the HVO troops, you would agree with me that that's the way it was officially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except MUP units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that officially Mr. Ramic was the superior to the HVO units. You would also agree with me that that was not the reality? Do you agree with both those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In reality, according to the chart, that is how it should have been. However, no order that was not signed by both Ramic and Dinko Zebic and latter Zdravko Sagolj was not valid for both structures, the TO and the HVO, unless the signatures of both commanders figured on those decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When was the war presidency formed in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if you'll believe me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated in your direct testimony what the law was regarding the appointment of commanders of the TO. You would agree with me, that until very recently, you did not know what the provisions of the law were, regarding the appointment of commanders of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, until recently my position was such that I had to be familiar with the law an all people's defence, that was my job. At the time that the Yugoslavia people's army existed and the territorial defence, as a separate component, that was part of the armed forces in the event of war, the commanders were appointed by the presidency or rather the presidency and the executive board at the time. With the formation of the territorial defence as the actual army of our state, we no longer had the JNA as our army, the JNA proved to be the aggressor, so the territorial defence could have immediately been called the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it inherited the name and the commanders of the staffs could be appointed only by the supreme command, of course, at the proposal of the presidency of that town, from which the commander of the municipal staff is to be appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that until recently you thought and, in fact, you stated that in the beginning of its existence, the war presidency both appointed and dismissed military commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of having said that, because I know that I, too, was appointed by the commander of the fourth corps to the post I held in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you still have some further questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I can just have one second to find something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that in your prior statement, you stated that before the direct link was established with the supreme command of the armed forces, that, the appointment and dismissal of commanders, was done by the war presidency of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I really am not aware of having said something like that, because the moment I was appointed chief of staff and when the new commander was appointed, Mr. Catic, this was not by the war presidency, and this was in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was Mr. Delalic a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, at a certain point in time, was in a military function and that is during the execution of Operation Oganj, when there was a bridge, a logistic bridge, to the units between Konjic. Mr. Kevric, myself and the units who were on the lines. That is the only military role that I'm aware of, and later as commander of TG1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question was, was he a member of the TO? That is the question. It's a simple one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have answered that question, sir. In June during the Operation Oganj, he did have a military function. He was in the TO. Later, he moved to TG-1, and until the end of his stay, in Konjic, until he left, he was in the TO because TG-1 is also part of the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your answer suggests that he was a member of the TO before he was appointed commander of TG-1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be said that he held a military function in Operation Oganj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Operation Oganj was before Mr. Delalic was appointed commander of Tactical Group 1? You have to say something so that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one month before he became commander of Tactical Group 1, which is the 27th of June, and TG-1 was at the end of July, beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to the operations, the military operations regarding Donje Selo and Bradina, you would agree with me that Mr. Delalic helped coordinate those operations, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot agree. I stated this when asked by the Defence. I'm certain that I never saw him during the operation at Donje Selo, nor did I hear him in communications, and I did not hear him during the Bradina operations either. I assumed that he was in Konjic. I presume that he could have been there. During the operations at Donje Selo, he was certainly not there, because I may have heard him during the Bradina operations, that he was there, I made have heard it from someone, but not at Donje Selo. As far as the coordination of such activities, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well sir, would you agree with me that the operation regarding Donje Selo and Bradina, in particular, let me just refer to Bradina, that was an operation to deblock the road to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To block or open?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: To deblock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to deblock, that is, to lift the blockade, to open up the road towards Sarajevo. That was the basic tenet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Units from outside Konjic took part in that operation, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some units from Tarcin and Pazaric, that is, from the upper side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that in your prior statement, referring to the operations to free the road to Sarajevo, you state: "I do know it was finally agreed that units from Konjic, Pazaric and Tarcin would take part, and some of the coordination was done by Zejnil Delalic." Sir, is that previously what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could have been only part of the coordination to have the units supplied with ammunition of a roundabout way, because we had enough of an ordnance in the Igman factory, and we had more than everybody else in Sarajevo, even Bosnia had at that time. I may have said it, but please understand, a number of years have passed and I cannot recall every single detail. I think that there have been more than two years since I made this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that you don't remember all the details about what Mr. Delalic did and did not do because of the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all details. I cannot -- if you will believe me, sometimes I cannot recall even the exact dates of where I was in certain periods, and I think that it's kind of normal for a person not to be able to remember every single detail. But as far as the period of 1992, I did not think about it very much, but when I found out that I was going to come here, then I reviewed certain documents, those certain documents that are in my possession, certain other documents that I had access to, so I did refresh my memory regarding this period of time that I'm testifying to. But, you know, once you start, you know, the tape starts rolling, as it were, and then you start remembering all kinds of details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, those documents that you reviewed to refresh your recollection, where are those documents now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of these documents are in my possession, as my personal archive, things that were sent to me as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Physically, are they in The Hague now or are they in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not here in The Hague. I did not consider it necessary to bring them along with me. It is my personal archives. These are my personal documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, given that you've used these to refresh your recollection, would you provide the Office of the Prosecutor access to those documents so that we may also review them, not necessarily now, but when you return? You have to say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If what I have, some of it is personal, so I don't think that all of it would be available, but the majority of it, yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to what you do and do not remember, you would agree with me that you do not know whether Mr. Delalic took part in the operation of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, as far as I know, and I know something about that situation because I had just joined the staff, I believe that he did not take part in the Bradina operation. I very often was present physically in the staff, and had he been present there, I think I would have heard his voice on the communications lines, because that is where the centre was. This is where the joint command was, a Rudar company. So I believe that had he taken part in this operation, I would have heard him at least once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your prior statement, you stated with respect to Bradina, "I really have no idea whether Zejnil Delalic took part in the actual combat operation." Did you say that in your prior statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this is what it says, if that is stated there, I probably said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct that you, yourself, don't know whether or not Mr. Delalic participated in the Bradina operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness already replied twice to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that Mr. Zvonko Zovko was the commander of the operations in Bradina at the end of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the position of Mr. Zovko in the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zovko was not a member of the joint command at that time. He was commander of a unit which numbered -- it was the largest unit in Konjic. That was the Podrasac or the Zubcanik. It was 800 strong and about 95 per cent were Muslim, because that was the composition of the local commune from which the unit came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was given authority over the Bradina operation, even though he was not a member of the joint command; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a field commander who was tasked with this job, with these additional units, and so he was the responsible commander in the field in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, Mr. Mucic requests your permission to leave to go to the restroom for two minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will grant that. He can go and come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the arrest of persons after the operations in Bradina, you stated that the bodies that would typically be charged with such matters would be the MUP and the military police. Sir, you would agree with me that you are not in a position to know whether, in fact, members of the TO also arrested persons after the operations in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the TO's military structure did not have its own military police. There was a number of Bosniak Muslims who were members of the HVO military police, but there was a MUP and there was the HVO military police who were in charge of arrests, detentions, because, according to the law, they were the only ones who could do these arrests, who could execute these arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, regardless of the law, you would agree with me that you don't know whether or not, as a matter of fact, certain members of the TO also arrested persons after the operations in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very likely that it could have happened, but maybe it could have been 15, 20 days later when the people, that is, the Serbs who were fleeing across mountains, would be captured. Then they would be captured by the military personnel at Igman, and then they would turn them over to the military police. If someone is captured, let's say if somebody jumps into a trench and captures someone, it is obvious that he would capture him, and then he would turn him over to the military police or to the police. If you find someone in a trench, you have to disarm the person and you have to keep them in some kind of detention until the proper legal authorities come and take over this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified in direct examination and earlier here this morning that you saw orders that were signed by both the TO and the HVO commanders. During the time that Mr. Delalic was coordinator, did you also have occasion to see orders signed by Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As coordinator?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three orders, perhaps, concerning logistic needs and when the train started running, and anything that related to what I was trying to explain to you before, something that had to do with our requests of the war presidency and what related to the war presidency's request in our regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 210, 213, and I think those should be sufficient for this present purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is very simple. When you were part of the TO, did you see those documents, Prosecution Exhibits 210 and 213?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This order of appointment I have never seen. I don't know what this is. And where Enver Redzepovic is mentioned, no, that order, I have never seen before. I have seen this other order, but I believe that this order was never fully implemented because Dinko Zebic's signature is missing, and this is what I said at that time. This is regarding the unit in which most personnel were actually Bosniak Muslims and their commander was Zvonko Zovko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, the witness has indicated he has never seen Prosecution Exhibit 210 before, but has seen Prosecution Exhibit 213 before. Now, sir, in addition to the HVO and the TO and the MUP forces in Konjic, were there also HOS units in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe in the latter part of August, HOS units may have appeared in the territory of the municipality and placed themselves under the command of the TO staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the Split Brigade, was there a brigade called the Split Brigade in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, there was a brigade, and it may have numbered about 100 to 200 men. In fact, these were local Croat people and some Muslim people who volunteered and placed themselves at the disposal to the Territorial Defence for the defence of Konjic. Soon thereafter, they left Konjic. In other words, they stayed in the Konjic area a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, moving forward now to Tactical Group 1, you talked about Tactical Group 1. Did you, yourself, ever see any order or orders appointing Mr. Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw it. I only heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that during the summer and fall of 1992, the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo was the main military goal for the defence forces of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Mr. Polutak had a car accident in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware of it from the fact that Zejnil Delalic was appointed to his position, but I don't know whether this was in August or July. So I do not know the exact period of time when this happened, but I know that Mr. Zejnil Delalic assumed his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. Polutak was to state that he had his car accident after Mr. Delalic was appointed commander of Tactical Group 1, that would be different than your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand this way of questioning. Mr. Polutak was never called as a witness, so I object to this way of framing the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness understands it. Did you misunderstand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what the question was. I think that it was a car accident of Mr. Polutak and the appointment of Mr. Delalic to the post of commander of TG, I don't know which came first. I believe that it could have happened in July. I could not swear on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Delalic was commander of Tactical Group 1, who was part of the Tactical Group 1 staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that in June of 1992, Mr. Sead Padalovic was commander of a unit that was sent to Tactical Group 1, which was then under the command of Mr. Polutak. My question is: For what period of time did that unit remain a subordinate part of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe seven to ten days at the most, because during the combat, during the fighting near Hadzici, we had four or five dead. Our unit came back and Commander Padalovic was also wounded during that fighting, and I think that that would mean that it would have been five to seven days all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1992, did you ever have occasion to see written orders from Mr. Delalic to the Konjic TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was only at the time when the supreme command transmitted this message regarding transfer of the Serb prisoners to Zenica. I think that that was the only time when I saw it, but if I saw a copy of the order, maybe I would refresh my memory. As it is right now, I really cannot state it with any kind of certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just move on, sir. You testified, in your direct, about a tension been the Konjic TO and Tactical Group 1 about a particular weapon. Can you tell us approximately when that dispute arose?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. The witness did not testify to this in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think in cross-examination, you can ask certain questions which can draw other answers. It's not necessarily limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you testify about some tension between the Konjic TO and Tactical Group 1 about a particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a brief misunderstanding because we considered this gun, 130 millimetre, was very important for the defence of Konjic. But after Sefer Halilovic's order came, he was, at the time, the commander of the armed forces, after his order came, we had to give it up, and this piece of weapon, this artillery piece, did leave the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand then that Sarajevo resolved the dispute by giving a direct instruction to municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only heard that we were to turn in this gun. And then we realised that when it was placed on a new position, that it would be too far to be part of the defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that during the summer and fall of 1992, Sarajevo was able to communicate directly with Konjic municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received most of the orders from the supreme command through TG-1 or TG-2, some through Hadzici, because through Mount Igman, there was a direct link with Sarajevo, and this was a way of communicating messages to the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir you mentioned that some soldiers from Konjic participated in Operation Oganj, and I believe you specifically mentioned that these soldiers were subordinate to the command of Tactical Group 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What units were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said, "Which units were these?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the units composed of several other units in the territory of municipality. Mr. Zlatan Redric was their commander, who after a brief preparation of this unit, led this unit to the area controlled by TG-2, and this unit took part in the liberation of the town of Trnovo and was very successful there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of the units that were subordinate to Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not a direct participant, but I did work on preparations of this unit, when it was leaving for this particular task and I was there to see them off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ramic part of the units that were subordinate to tactical group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the order that these troops should be subordinated to tactical group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on the basis of an order of the supreme command. Because, at that time, the supreme command was sort of making assessments where they needed troops. We -- they asked of us for certain units and this was similar to the case of Mr. Padalovic and his unit, so, TG-2. It is probably the TG-2 command that asked for a certain number of soldiers and then probably the order was issued to us to fill the need of them with a number of soldiers from our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "probably", I assume you don't know as a matter of fact how it happened, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I know whether this was planned in the supreme command headquarters, but I know exactly on which requests, on whose request we send the units. And I am not aware of the communications between the supreme command and TG-1, but I know that we received the order of the supreme command headquarters to set aside some units and transfer them to the area of TG-2's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case, sir? KARIBI-WHYTE: Mr. McHenry, we would like to break now and reassemble at two o'clock for you to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seats and then the Prosecution will now continue with its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tahirovic. Mr. Tahirovic, you talked a little bit this morning about how the Konjic municipal headquarters normally received orders. Can you tell us, did the orders from the supreme command to Konjic headquarters, were they usually transmitted through Tactical Group 1 or Tactical Group 2 or did the orders usually go directly to municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, it would happen that some orders to the municipal staff would arrive through Fojnica, through Zagreb, and, if you can believe this, from the United States as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, starting in the end of July going through November, were the orders to municipal headquarters normally transmitted through Tactical Group 1 or 2 or were they normally directed, directly to municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When there was a possibility to cross the runway in Sarajevo, we would receive some of those orders, but a large number of these orders also were received through Tactical Groups 1 and 2. In other words, when the couriers were able to get the messages across the runway in Sarajevo, we were then able to get those messages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Tactical Group 2 created?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you go to that, what sort of orders do you have in mind which went to TG-1. There may be different types of orders. Some may be coming through TG-1. Some may be coming directly. You have not clarified that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were was there any kind of distinction between the kind of orders that would go through Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were different kinds of orders and there was no clear distinction which come through Tactical Group 1 or 2. There was no selection of that type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Tactical Group 2 created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical Group 2, I think, exists as long as Tactical Group 1 on Igman, and the first commander as far as I know was Mirsad Tatic. Upon the liberation of Trnovo, Tactical Group 3 was formed. All of it was aimed to improve conditions for lifting the siege of Sarajevo. I don't know whether you know, but until the end of the war, we were trying to lift the siege. Unfortunately, we didn't manage through military means. It was done through political means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, did I understand that to your understanding, Tactical Group 2 was created at the same time as Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical Group 1, there was Tactical Group Visoko, then there was one in Pazaric. There was one in Igman. That is Tactical Group 2, whose area extended roughly from Igman, but the people who were involved would know better. The road across Igman, overlooking Sarajevo, that was Tactical Group 2. Pazaric was mount Orman and the area towards Kiseljak, that belonged to Tactical Group 1, and there was Tactical Group Visoko around the town of Visoko. Therefore, all the forces involved in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo were divided in this way, to facilitate command and control of units participating in lifting the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you know whether or not Tactical Group 2 was created at the same time as Tactical Group 1? If you don't know, you can just say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of Tactical Group 1 located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delalic's house in Konjic also used and referred to as Tactical Group 1 command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as Mr. Delalic's house is concerned, I'm very familiar with that because I later became commander and after some unfortunate circumstances when some things were stolen from that house, I reacted and restored the house to the family. In the lower part of the building was a high quality communications centre with several Motorolas, stationary, radio transmitters of ultra short-wave and short-wave transmitters. This communication centre was there, and to protect the building, we accommodated our military police there, so that nobody should appropriate the house, but despite that, this happened, and I ordered when I became commander, that the house be restored to the rightful owners and I apologised to the family and the owners because of the things that had been stolen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the communication centre a communication centre for the municipal headquarters, for the Tactical Group or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We also had a separate communication centre in the The Third of March School and later in the hotel, but because this was high quality, the equipment was very good, it was kind of a relay station between us and our units. Until we captured Mount Zlata (phoen), we were not able to communicate well with Glavoticevo and other areas, with our units, so this centre was something we used very frequently, and the people manning this centre would convey to us, very often, the messages sent to them from our units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you listen very carefully to my question. If it can be answered simply with a yes or no, please do so and don't explain unless somehow it's necessary to answer the question. My question was: Was the communication centre used by the TO, the Tactical Group 1 or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question. Both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 108/1. This is already in evidence, but I have extra copies for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is this called?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's a document about Mr. Delalic's house in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, first of all, this document, the typed signature says Commander Catic. Tell me, do you recognise whose signature is actually on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you would agree with me that this document refers to Mr. Delalic's house and refers to it as the facility of the formal Tactical Group 1 command. Would you agree with me about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's probably an error, that it has not been said that the communication centre was in this part of the house. He does, indeed, say here that it is the command of TG-1, but it is a communication centre. If you have other documents, then you will see from the inventory that this was, indeed, a communications centre from Harrison, Motorola and the other equipment held there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did I understand you correctly that other than the brief period of time when Mr. Padalovic's unit was subordinated to Tactical Group 1 under Mr. Polutak from May to December 1992, there were never any other units from Konjic, who were subordinates to Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only unit from Konjic that was subordinated to Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the only unit -- I'm sorry. Is it the case that all the troops from Konjic who participated in JUG '92, were subordinate to either Tactical Group 1 or Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Tactical Group. I think this has been explained here, at least judging by the people who came here before me, is a temporary formation set up for a particular operation. If you want me to answer with yes or no, then I would say that not a single unit was subordinated to Tactical Group 1 or 2, except when it was formed to perform a particular task. If I may clarify this, throughout the time of the war, we had our front-lines, which was about 100 to 150 kilometres long, to defend the Konjic area from the SDS, armed bands and later the HVO. So that we had very serious problems. And in spite of so many troops, sometimes we had fewer troops than we needed, so that we could not afford to give our units to someone else, to have command over them, except if this was ordered by the supreme command for a particular task. Because the aim of all citizens, and especially us in Konjic, was to lift the blockade of Sarajevo so as to be able to link up with our leadership and the capital of our country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, sir, let me ask. What did you mean by saying judging by the people here before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are you driving at? Let's get to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is: Is it the case that all the troops from Konjic who participated in JUG '92, at the time they were participating in JUG '92, were they subordinate to either Tactical Group 1 or Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the unit under the command of Zlatan Redzic. However, all of us had certain tasks assigned to us by the supreme command, that is, to strengthen the defence lines, to take care not to allow the Chetniks to attack our units from behind, and we were under the command of our staff, the TO staff. Only the unit and a Captain Zlatan Redzic were directly subordinated, whereas, the other units carried out tasks which contributed to a certain degree, to the execution of operations successfully in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, let's get your answer clear. Which of the units in the Konjic area was subordinate to TG-1, because you've indicated all of those in separate ways were carrying out the instructions of the supreme command. Which was directly subordinated to TG-1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In operation south, as madam has asked, JUG '92, not a single unit was subordinated to Tactical Group 1 but to Tactical Group 2, and this was the unit headed by Mr. Zlatan Redzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that other than this one unit that you have referred to, that was headed by Mr. Redzic, other than that, were there other units from Konjic who participated in JUG '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Konjic, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask that -- just may I ask that Prosecution Exhibit 99-10 be shown to the witness? 99-7-10. Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to paragraph 5 of the order from Mr. Delalic dated 24th August, 1992. First of all, let me ask, have you ever seen this order before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I've seen it but I don't know exactly when. If this is the date, the 24th of August, that I didn't see it at that very time, because from the 24th until the 30th, I was absent. I was visiting my family, but after that, I'm sure that I did see this order because I was working on the preparation of this unit for going in the direction of Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand you to mean to say that you assumed you must have seen this, but at the present time, you don't have any specific recollection of having seen it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen it. I just can't remember the date when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Directing, sir, your attention to paragraph 5 of the order. You would agree with me that that indicates that troops from Konjic are to be used as part of operation JUG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I explained a moment ago the role of the other units within the territory of Konjic municipality linked to the operation JUG. We provided security support for the rear and the sides of the units participating in operation JUG. Those were our lines anyway, lines that we held, but we just had to reinforce fire power on the basis of this order to engage enemy forces and prevent them from being transferred to Tactical Group 1, 2, and other Tactical Groups that were on the offensive around the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me if I've understood you correctly and this is a fair summary, that, to your knowledge, there were no troops that were specifically assigned to be subordinate to Mr. Delalic, but that all the troops in Konjic were used in some way as part of operation JUG; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but on the basis of the order of the supreme command, all the units in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had such a task. This happened repeatedly and it was our duty to engage enemy forces through higher fire power, to pretend that we would attack and, in fact, we would attack elsewhere. This is a well-known practise in all the armies of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would agree with me, that in supporting Operation JUG, in the way you've just talked about, the Konjic troops were responsible to Mr. Delalic for the carrying out of those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but to the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, let me direct your attention to the last sentence of that order and does it not say that Mr. Ramic is responsible to Mr. Delalic for implementation of the order? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand this order as a transcript of the order of the supreme command. This is what we would receive through TG-1 and through TG-2 and in other similar ways we would receive orders of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my specific question was, you would agree with me that the order states that Mr. Ramic is responsible to Mr. Delalic for implementation of the order, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says here, but it cannot be correct. It must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am correct that the supplies and the equipment for tactical Group 1 were kept in Celebici, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of the equipment and supplies, not for Tactical Group 1. We were assisting them. We would give them our equipment. As a tactical group they didn't have their own equipment, they didn't have their own units. But very frequently we would assist them with the reserves that we had. I told you that at the beginning of the war in Konjic, at the factory, there were several million bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the later part of July, August, September and October of 1992, how frequently did you yourself, have contact with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I hadn't seen him at all. In July, maybe once or twice I spoke to him over the radio links. On one occasion, Major Kevric when we need to equip an anti-aircraft unit which was to have been sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't really need you to explain your answers, I just need you to answer the question. Now, sir, during its existence from May to December of 1992, was Celebici a military prison, a civilian prison or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very difficult to explain in hindsight. It wasn't civilian in the sense that civilians would detained there. But it was civilian, because the MUP, even though it was an armed component, was in control. Then, for a time, it was under the control of the HVO. And then for a time we were together. So it's very difficult to say. People were held in Celebici, who, upon capture, had arms on them. In other words, they were soldiers. So it cannot be considered a civilian prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you already talked about who was the commander of the camp and your lack of knowledge about it in June and July of 1992. How about for the period from August until November, who was the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago when you asked me that upon arrival and that was the first and only time I entered the area where prisoners were held that we were welcomed by Hazim Delic and Mr. Sdravko Mucic. And, as far as I remember, no, he was in fact introduced to me at the end of August, beginning of September, as the prison commander, or actually, barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Mr. Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Mr. Esad Landzo later, though he lives in my neighbourhood. He's a brother, who at the time resembled one another. I don't know whether they're really twins, but they were so alike that I couldn't distinguish between the two. His brother is still living in Konjic and now when I look at Esad Landzo you can tell the difference. But in those days, his brother is still thin and he has gained weight, so his face has changed, but I met him somewhere in '93 when I became commander and when the prison was set up in Unit A004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how did you meet in 1993 when the prison was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand, are you talking about August '92? Are you asking me who I met then in August, '92, when I went there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that I met him somewhere in 1993 and I am asking whether or not you're asking about Mr. Esad Landzo or his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about Esad Landzo. I know that it is Esad Landzo, but physically throughout the war I could not distinguish between the two. And as I was just saying, when I look at him now and brother then, I can tell the difference. But they were so similar in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you point out by identifying an article of clothing that he's wearing who Mr. Esad Landzo is? KARIBI-WHYTE: I don't really understand, he says he can know the difference, but at that time was difficult to distinguish two, what are you asking that for?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just trying to clarify that this person this witness knows is Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He told you, he had said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of Mr. Esad Landzo's brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know him by his nickname, Zenga - that is Esad Landzo. And I still don't know his brother's name. From the papers and all these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified about your opinion that Mr. Delalic did not, as far as you knew, have a position of superior authority regarding the prison. I presume then that you are in a position to know who did have superior authority and I would just ask that you tell us every person who was a superior with respect to the Celebici prison from May to December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
