utterances.text: I really can't tell you by name because I don't know. I told you that Mr. Delalic, in view of the posts he held, he could not have been the commander or the superior for the Celebici camp. I told you at the beginning of the war, a MUP unit was based there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case that you can't give us the name of any person who was a superior with respect to the Celebici prison from May to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You spoke about the commander and now you're speaking about something about the commander. He was responsible for setting up the prison and he was responsible for the protection of the prison and the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give us the name of every person who had authority besides the camp commander who you have already mentioned who had authority over the Celebici prison? And if you don't know the names, just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know because it was not within the domain of work and my responsibilities. And I told you what my job was, it was preparation for combat activities and training for combat operations. So I was very busy and I did not know at that time, nor did I have particular interest in who was the commander of the, of the camp or the prison Celebici and who was in charge there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, please tell us exactly what entity or entities had responsibility for the Celebici prison between May and December of 1992. And, please, if you specify for what period of time any particular entity had responsibility for the Celebici prison, if you know. If you don't know, just please tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as MUP is concerned, I really don't know which parties at the MUP were in charge of these duties. As far as the TO and the HVO are concerned, it is really the security body, it is the only body that can be in charge of such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, can you tell us for what period of time between May and December 1992, the MUP had some involvement, had some responsibility for the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, were you satisfied with that answer? Because he hasn't said definitely anybody was in charge. Is it any news that the security branch might be in charge. He didn't say they were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what entities had responsibility for Celebici prison or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just told you how it was supposed to have looked, but in reality I do not know who was responsible. I don't know the hierarchy at the MUP. I don't know the departments there, the structure. I don't know how it is structured. And in the joint command, that is the joint TRNA command (phoen), it is only the security body that could have been in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stick with MUP first. I am not asking you for a particular name or even a particular division within the MUP. But is it your testimony, sir, that for some period of time the MUP was involved and had responsibility for the Celebici prison camp? If you know for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, they had to. Yes, I know that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the MUP have responsibility for Celebici? For what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that this was early on, but I don't know until when and I don't know when this responsibilities were transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You a security wing and similarly the joint command of the security wing, which of the two, or jointly the two, had the responsibility? MUP had a security branch, so has the joint command of the TO and HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that in the period -- during the period when I was offered to become commander at Celebici, I know that there was a special MUP unit was stationed there, deployed there and -- because there were certain Serbs with whom certain illegal weapons were found. I know that this was a MUP type of activity, so I did not want to become involved in that. And -- but now I cannot say when this responsibility may have -- been transferred from MUP to someone else. By the time that I joined the TO headquarters, we had nothing to do with the Celebici prison. And I don't know at what point, the 43rd brigade took over control. I don't when it became -- it had been and the 4th quarter became in charge of it, so I really cannot speak to that and I really can't tell you at which point in time any of this transfer of authority took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This prison at Celebici is not a private prison, it's a prison of the state, so somebody must be responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also believed that somebody had to be in charge, but I don't know about that. Only people who are specialists in military things, they can tell you. But the positions that I had, oh, yes, was one of the busiest ones because it involves all the preparations of all the units. So, at that time, I was very busy doing that and I was not paying much attention to which body was in charge of that. And also, I just cannot tell you when it was transferred, that responsibility from whom and to whom. And I really cannot say when it happened. Somebody else may have this information, but I certainly do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether or not at some point and, if so, when, the HVO had some responsibility for the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO did not have its own military police. I'm sorry, I keep confusing the army and the territorial defence. The territorial defence established its military police in the later half of August -- well, actually in the beginning of August. So in early August we did not have our own military police. And throughout this period, among the people who were working in -- as security in the Celebici barracks, these were the TO people and the HVO people. And I don't know -- they had to have something because they had units who were equipped for such attacks. That is, they did have military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, are you saying that at various points, both the TO and the HVO had responsibility for Celebici, but you have no idea when and you have no idea how it worked in reality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He answered that question, he said he was too busy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am just trying to confirm since in his direct testimony he made some much broader statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you're saying at various points, both the TO and the HVO had responsibility for Celebici prison, but you have no idea when and you have no idea how for the responsibility worked and practised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a while, it was the case and, as I told you, throughout this period, there were, the TO and the HVO members who were working at the Celebici barracks in security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, I assume you have no information about to whom the camp commander reported in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me in 1992, there were no regulations governing the setting up and operation of prisons of military prisons such as Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the law on people's defence of the Yugoslavia, the TO could not have prisons, only the Yugoslav people's army could have prisons. And whoever the territorial defence members would capture, they would turn them over to the jail. In other words, at that time, by regulations, the TO could not have its own prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And you would agree with me that as the TO was turned into the Bosnian army, that there were, at least in 1992, there were not regulations set up to resolve how military prisons should be handled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that the Prosecutor's office, the court in Honacu (phoen) did not function. And we did not have a military court, it was in Sarajevo. We had a basic court in Konjic. We have a district court in Mostar. But I know for my studies, we had a course in this, so I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if you would agree with this, sir. You would agree that in 1992, in May to December of 1992, the matter of who ran the prisons was resolved as a matter of practice rather than as a matter of law or regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know. It is possible, but I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. You testified in direct that you and others repeatedly drew attention to the Konjic soldiers to the need for respect of the law and humane treatment of all persons. What was done to ensure that the persons who worked in Celebici understood the need to respect the law and treat the prisoners humanely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how that is connected with Celebici. I know when preparing for combat operations, I know that one of the orders was always concerning the treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you don't know with respect to Celebici, which is what my question was, all you have to say is, I don't know, with respect to Celebici. Thank you. Now, sir, who on the TO staff had the duty to investigate and report on what was happening in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of any report with respect to Celebici that is during the meetings of -- on different kinds of preparations, which I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Celebici considered a matter of some significance to the command of the TO or to the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that it was supposed to be anything very significant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified in direct testimony, something about the capture of Dr. Grubac, do you know why Dr. Grubac was in prison in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he fled his post in the health centre and he went up to Bradina where his father-in-law had a summer house. This is what they told me in 1993. They told me that they were captured on Mount Igman and that from there, they were brought to Celebici. This may have been ten days after the end of the Brighton (phoen) operation. He and his brother-in-law, Dobrivoje Dordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the reason Dr. Grubac was in prison in Celebici was because he fled his post in the health centre and went to Bradina? Sir, my question had been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not what I said. He was already in Bradina when the combat operations start. When we captured Bradina, he attempted to escape and he was captured in Mount Igman, so he was a soldier by then, not a physician who he was when he left the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know he was a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do we know if somebody was a soldier? What would somebody, especially a Serb, what would he be doing behind our forces? So it is quite possible, I say, that he or his brother-in-law may have carried weapons at that time. And that's how you recognise whether somebody is a soldier. He wouldn't have been a hunter in May and June of 1992 if he were found with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Dr. Grubac was found with weapons, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who released Dr. Grubac from Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not getting an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked with him in health centre in Konjic. He was an ear, nose, eye specialist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was detained in Celebici also, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he used to live close to me and we talked. I saw him one day during that summer. He told me that he was captured and then that he was released. But he also did not tell me who released him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were there women detained in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that from May to December of 1992 you heard no reports or rumours of mistreatment of detainees in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Delalic interviewed on television about the reports of mistreatment of detainees in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that it was known by persons, including yourself, that Celebici was not a safe place for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Safe in what sense? Safe from shelling or...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the persons detained in Celebici had reason to fear for their bodily safety?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He answered your question and he asked you to explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that it was known by persons, including yourself, that Celebici was not a safe place and that persons might physically mistreat the detainees by beating them or torturing them or killing them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of that. I know that they were transferred to Celebici in the beginning specifically for safety reasons because the prison at Musala, which was the MUP's prison, that this was constantly shelled, and so they were facing much more danger, whereas in Celebici, they were far away from the shelling. As far as I could tell, they were quite safe over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me that you intervened to protect Miro Golubovic because you believed he was in danger while in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not dangers from within. See, he had just come back from Tisovica, and this gentleman, Mr. Sadil Dzumhur told me, after the death of our nine soldiers, that is policeman at Bradina, the anti-Serb mood in the town had risen and that some old wounds were re-opened. And certain friends of Mr. Niksic and Mr. Boric had been killed and wanted to go there and Miro Golubovic was fingered as one of the persons, who was suspected as one of the persons, who may have been involved in that. So I went to protect him because there was a danger for him from outside, not from within. Because when we heard while at Tisovica of this case, immediately, it was said that the Chetniks had done it. We heard this on the radio, and since units that were out of my command in Sunji, and Zukici, they immediately wanted to go there, a very bad climate was created. Imagine if nine people perished in such a way under circumstances that were not very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that the detainees in Celebici were known to have reason to fear for their safety, in that persons from outside the camp, would be allowed into the camp to mistreat them; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that did not happen, but you could not preclude a possibility that somebody would be able to do that. We wanted to make sure that whenever somebody was captured or taken prisoner, and this is what we cared about a lot throughout the war, we did not want to come into a situation when something unforeseen would happen, but that everything would be done in accordance with the Geneva conventions. Everybody had that flyer with those rules, but you could not control individuals. If somebody lost someone close to him, you could not preclude a possibility. This would be a concern that would also relate to the Serbs who had stayed in town and those in the Celebici prison especially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sir, you would agree with me that the reason Mr. Golubovic was in danger was because of the possibility that other persons from outside the prison camp might come in and do him serious bodily harm. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, they were members of the special police of the MUP, very well-trained and capable people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my specific question, and I ask if you can answer it with a yes or no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have given you a specific answer, those people could, probably could and, who knows, maybe they wouldn't succeed, but I didn't want to leave anything to chance. Maybe they wouldn't have done anything, but I didn't want this to happen because this was an acquaintance of mine, and I consulted my superior commander and that was the decision we took and I've already explained to the Defence how we dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at this time, surely you didn't think Mr. Golubovic was the only person in the entire camp who was in danger, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of him only. I didn't hear of anyone else, nor did I hear any rumour about anybody else being at risk. I must tell you that later, I learned of the killing, that is, the only death I learned of, Mr. Klimenta, because that too was a friend of mine, and an acquaintance, but I heard that this was an accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to Mr. Golubovic. If I understood your testimony, it was your belief that Mr. Golubovic was the only detainee in danger in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, that was how I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you went to talk to Mr. Cerovac who told you you should send certain forms to his command post, about Mr. Golubovic. When was this, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't go to talk with Mr. Cerovac. I spoke to him over the radio because he was very far away from me. This could have been the second half of July, because I spent four or five days at Tisovica and I left around the 10th, I think, and when I came back, I learned about it. So this must have been mid-July or the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this during the time that Mr. Delalic was coordinator or the time he was commander of Tactical Group 1, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Delalic was still at Vranske Stijene when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been during the period he was coordinator, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While he was at the Vranske Stijene, he was a soldier of the Territorial Defence, I've already told you, responsible for logistics and radio relay station. Because, in view of where he was, he couldn't coordinate anything. He had to have contacts again via radio and through us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that when Mr. Delalic was at Vranske Stijene, he was no longer a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can do is make an assumption. I know that his role was a logistics man or somebody working in the rear at Vranske Stijene. I know of his role that he had when we had any contact. And according to the tasks he performed, that is all he could have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what exactly did you do after your talk with Mr. Cerovac with respect to the release of Mr. Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just took the papers from the headquarters, two papers. I can't remember exactly what was written on them, and I sent them via a messenger to Vranske Stijene. No, not Vranske Stijene. I think Mr. Cerovac was at Glavotic then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly did you get these papers? Where was the headquarters that you got these papers located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff at that time was headquartered in The Third of March Elementary School. These were joint premises. Some were separate but this was in the headquarters where all the other papers are kept; clean paper and other papers ready for further processing. They were responsible for copying them and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the TO commander, to your knowledge, have authority to release prisoners from Celebici at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Cerovac did with those documents afterwards, but all I know is that two or three or five days later, I saw Mr. Golubovic who came to the street where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that it was Mr. Delalic who signed his release document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To tell you the truth, I didn't have any more contact with him because very soon after that, this man left Konjic, and the assumption is, that with the help of the HVO, he crossed Kobiljaca and went into Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides talking with Mr. Cerovac, did you talk to anyone else about Mr. Golubovic or the conditions in the prison, such as the head of the MUP or the war presidency or the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't. I asked my superior for his advice because I didn't have the authority to do that. My competencies were very clear. I was involved with the defence of the town. This was more of a private initiative on my part, than my official duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was something done to advise the head of the MUP that his soldiers were believed to be putting detainees in Celebici at risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't inform the head of the MUP because this was a story told by Mr. Diksa, which was not verified, and as I didn't want to leave anything to chance, that is why I reacted. I couldn't accuse anyone without proof. I just wanted to prevent the possibility of any such thing happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that you escorted members of a delegation, you believe members of an OSCE delegation to Celebici and that your driver made a remark about the prisoners looking like actors. Did the driver accompany you and Major Kevric during the tour of Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were driven by Major Kevric's driver, Alic, and escorting this delegation was an HVO policeman from Mostar, and it was he who said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not understand the remark about looking like actors. How did you understand the remark about the prisoners looking like actors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that their appearance was normal, they hadn't been beaten. They were not bruised. They were not in tatters. They had went to sleep and he just said if only you could see ours, then you would understand. The point was that their appearance was normal. Just when we arrived, about ten of them were shaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that previously in June of 1996 when you gave your statement to the Defence, you did not know the identity of the delegation, and you thought it was probably Helsinki watch. Why do you now know or believe it was an OSCE delegation rather than Helsinki watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I made my statement within ten minutes, and I couldn't really mention all the details. I explained to you a moment ago, I've been thinking hard about this situation for the past two years, and especially so, the last two months, because for all of us coming here, this is a great stress, all of us who have never had anything to do with a court or the police. So I have hardly been sleeping this past two months. So I wasn't quite sure whether it was a humanitarian organisation or something like that, and I think that is what I said in my statement. The leader of the group was a tall, well-built dark-skinned man. They said he was an American, and I remember him because of his figure, and he stuck in my mind. He appeared to be in charge of that group of people who came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone suggest to you that it was an OSCE delegation, rather than a Helsinki watch delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they came, they probably introduced themselves. I don't know how I...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to find out why in June of 1996, you thought it was Helsinki watch and now you believe it was OSCE. My question is, did someone suggest to you that it was an OSCE delegation and not a Helsinki watch delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody suggested it to me, no. I said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it just came to you of your own accord that it was OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even when I made that statement, and I think the investigator will confirm that I wasn't sure. I mentioned OSCE and the Helsinki watch. I didn't think it was very important. The important thing was that there was a delegation and that was the first time I had entered the prison. I didn't think that to be important or less important, because Helsinki watch is also concerned with human rights protection. So, I wasn't sure even then, I was hesitant, and then I left this word, the name of the Helsinki watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Helsinki watch also published a report, very critical of Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen anyone's report of the Helsinki watch, the OSCE or the Red Cross. Later on, I frequently had contact with someone, I know he is Swiss. He would come often for a cup of coffee at the motel where our command was. But no one ever said anything, nor did I see any written document or a report on bad conditions because that wouldn't correspond to the truth. If anybody were to say that the conditions were bad, that would not correspond to the truth, at the time in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know what the conditions in Celebici were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I entered the hangar with that delegation. And I saw how the people looked. I saw blankets folded in the form of beds and I may have stayed there five or six minutes in that hangar. After that, I and Mr. Kevric were asked to go out because they wanted to talk to them alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who arranged for the visits of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who organised it. I just know about the later period when this Swiss gentleman visiting Musala would come by to the command building to have a coffee. There was a young lady with him from Mostar, an interpreter, so we would meet quite often to have coffee together, rather than dealing with any difficulties, but that was afterwards, after the transfer from Celebici to Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the TO ever unwilling to let the Red Cross into the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that we had nothing to conceal in the Celebici prison. I'm not aware of any such possibility, because in the BiH army, I later had the position of liaison officer with such organisations, and I can tell you that a large number of parcels went through me and then to Musala, and very often, every week, a Red Cross team would come from Sarajevo to visit them, bringing them food and clothing and...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you listen to my question and just answer my question. Between August and November of 1992, to whom did the Red Cross send their reports about Celebici camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either the Red Cross of Konjic or the international Red Cross, which one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The international Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably to their own superiors. How do I know? I suppose they have their own superiors. I don't know. My short answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your direct examination, you stated in answer to a question by His Honour Karibi-Whyte, that the TO received an order from the supreme command to speed up the process of the interrogation of the Celebici prisoners. Do you remember that? You have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When approximately was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was either mid-September or the second half of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the supreme command staff, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you know for sure or is that just an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for sure that it is from the supreme command. Whether it came to me through TG-2 or TG-1, I couldn't tell. If you have a document and show it to me...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. Is it this one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says TG-1 and I think I've explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Is that the document you're referring to, the order to speed up the process of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under point 1 of this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that document from Mr. Delalic orders the TO to immediately conduct interrogations. Can you please tell me what the TO did in response to this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As this is an order of the supreme command, I know that we answered to the supreme command that we couldn't do it, and we asked that those prisoners be transferred to Mostar or Zenica where there are spacious prisons, where there are courts operating, that they should be dislocated there, that a final investigation be carried out, a trial to be organised, and the supreme command answered that it would be Zenica, that Mostar was exposed to shelling and the situation had already worsened, in relations between the TO and the HVO in Mostar. But I know that we didn't manage even then to transfer the prisoners to Zenica because the HVO held Kiseljak and prevented the movement of our forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when the TO was responding to this order of August 24th, did they respond through Tactical Group 1, since the document came from -- since the order came from Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, why couldn't the interrogations be speeded up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, in Konjic, did not have any judicial bodies to do that, because I said at the very beginning, the military investigating commission was formed, headed by its president, Goran Lokas who was then responsible for security in the joint command. Why they didn't do that and how, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown 99-7-11, which is the order of 28th of August? Sir, this is the order dated the 28th of August from Mr. Delalic to Mr. Mucic. Did you see that document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't. I told you at that time I wasn't there and that also is an order of the supreme command, and if it had to do with the manager of the Celebici prison, then it must have been passed on to him. I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you talked about this commission set up, the military investigation commission. You're aware that Mr. Sacir Pajic was a member of the military investigation committee, that had been created in June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't aware that Mr. Pajic was a member of the military investigation committee set up in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of Mr. Pajic, only just before the beginning of the war, that he was the first soldier in the Yugoslav war to be wounded in Slovenia as a lower ranking officer and of the JNA, and he was undergoing treatment somewhere and I met him much later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand then that in June of 1992, you were not aware that Mr. Paic was a member of the military investigation committee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see him in the joint command headquarters, but I didn't know that he was on the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did know that Mr. Paoic was a member of the joint command, correct? You have to answer yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sorry. He was present in the headquarters. I was there, perhaps, most frequently because of my job, but people would come and go and I assumed he was a member of the joint command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just ask you. In direct examination you authenticated a chart shown to you by Ms. Residovic, Document 166, in which Mr. Paoic's name was mentioned. I assume then that you, in fact, don't know whether or not this chart is correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What, did want him to say, to authenticate the chart to somebody? He has already done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness, himself, did it and I am just bringing out that, in fact, although this witness authenticated, he is now stating that he doesn't know whether or not certain people were or were not a member of the joint committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He's authenticated it, then that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I do apologise. Yes, but those changes occurred frequently, so I cannot claim whether he was in the military investigations commission, but he was in the building and he was there. And for as long as there was a municipal staff and the brigade, he was always in the commands. Even the two of us worked together in the 4th core and in the 6th core, so maybe at that particular time he held some other post. I am not sure whether he was just then appointed to the military investigations commission. That's all I wanted to say because there are people there who were killed. Then there were people who held one position at one time and then they were moved to another position. And I said that in answering my question and in authenticating the document because even the commanders, I am the 7th commander, the 7th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Mr. Delalic worked together with the military investigating committee in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, you have no idea why Mr. Paoic and the other members of the military investigating committee decided that they could not continue their work in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't even know that they decided not to continue working until this order of the supreme command came to finish things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when the order came from the supreme command to finish things, I assume that some inquiry was done to find out why the first committee had not finished things, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, somebody probably did that and what they did and how they did it, I am unable to say here now. We all had our own tasks. I couldn't interfere with somebody else's work. There were things discussed at joint meetings, but most things that were happening in other bodies, I was not familiar with, if they were less important or had their normal course of procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who decided within the TO headquarters that the interrogations could not be speeded up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end it was the commander who decides, but in agreement with the other members of the staff. So the decisions are taken at briefings and meetings, but in the final analysis every decision has to be taken by the commander upon the proposal of his. That's why these services exist, to help the commander in his work. So probably at the proposal of one of these services, probably the security service, and he decided that this could not be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you say "probably", does that mean that you, in fact, don't know how it was decided or who decided it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you explicitly, I am just telling you what the procedure is. I can't know everything, every single detail as to what happened at that time. Maybe I didn't attend one of those meetings, but I know most of the documents because I saw them. But who exactly passed a certain document, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, even later on in December of 1992, there was another commission set up to conduct military investigations, correct, of the prisoners in Celebici and Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in January '93 because I know an order came from the 4th core command, which had already been formed in the meantime and the prisoners were all transferred from Celebici to Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were involved with that commission, setting up that commission, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly. You see, upon the formation of the staff when Mr. Musad Catic was appointed, a post was in the search for a deputy commander and Mr. Dragan Andric held that post. And I had the post of chief of staff. And I was mostly responsible for combat operations and he stood in for the commander. Our commander was wounded and he was absent frequently. He was wounded in the leg and he was absent. So maybe in his absence I may have signed a document or two, but as we see on this document about Zejnil Delalic's house, it says for or on behalf of the commander of the TO staff or perhaps Mr. Mucic at that time was participating in a new attempt to deblock set him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we're about to rise and come back at 4:00 p.m. to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I apologise for being a few minutes late. I had to speak on another matter. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat. Yes, Ms. McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware in November 1992, Mr. Delic took over as commander of Celebici camp, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that starting in the latter part of November and the beginning part of December that the municipal headquarters of the TO began to be actively involved in Celebici and Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 45th brigade had already been established under the name of Neretvica (phoen), and I know that after the fourth corps was established, it took responsibility for providing security for that portion of the Celebici barracks. We received an order by the command of the fourth corps since this was to become a real barracks in every sense of the word, that these persons should be transferred from Celebici to Musala. So that with the assistance of the Red Cross, we converted the locker rooms in the Musala sports hall for prison use. In December 1992, Celebici were evacuated, that is, all the prisoners from Celebici were transferred to Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that in the latter part of November, you, yourself, had a conversation with Mr. Delic where Mr. Delic indicated to the effect that, "Since I'm now under the command of the Territorial Defence, what are we to do with the prisoners?" Do you remember have a conversation like that with Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that this conversation did not take place, but I personally do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree with me that in the latter part of November, a commission was sent into Celebici to ascertain the state of the prison and ascertain, among other things, the health of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the fourth corps command in the latter part of November or early December established a commission which investigated some other things in the Konjic municipality. People from Mostar came to investigate the unsolved murders of nine policemen, the wounding of Mr. Mirsad Catic, certain looting and robberies, and I'm not aware of the fact of this commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just direct you to the question. Are you aware that in November of 1992, a commission was sent in from municipal headquarters, was sent in to Celebici to ascertain the state of the prison and the state of the health of the prisoners? Were you aware or not aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean a medical commission? Was this a medical commission you're referring to? I think that this could have happened after the order of the fourth corps commander, when the order was issued to transfer the prisoners to the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, I think in cross-examination, you are allowed to lead him. If you want a particular answer and think he have that, I'll permit a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown from the Defence exhibits an attachment 5D/51, and I have extra copies if that would assist things. Sir, I ask you, first of all, do you recognise whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this is a signature of Mr. Esad Senic who, at the time, was on duty. Let's see, 5 December, I think this is some kind of a mistake because I think at this time he already was with the 45th brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see this document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but this could be what I was referring to. This is the transfer of responsibility of the prisoner between the 45th brigade of which Mr. Memic (phoen) was a commander and the municipal headquarters. This is to identify the -- it says to establish the state of affairs. That may not mean only the prisoners. It means all the equipment of the facilities, things like that. So it could mean the transfer of control of the prison between the 45th brigade and the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you see the report created by this commission which refers to the equipment and to the health of the prisoners? Did you ever see the report that this commission came up with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the report, but I see that the late Dr. Stojanovic also examined all the prisoners, because within a day or two, they were transferred from Celebici to Musala, so probably this is why this commission was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would also agree with me, sir, that in January, a decision was made that the prisoners' interrogations should finally be completed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown Defence document 7-1. I have extra copies for Your Honours, since it's been awhile since we had this exhibit. Now, sir, whose signature is that under where the commander normally signs? Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could be my signature, but it looks more like a bad imitation of my signature, but I'm aware of the fact that such commission was established, but I'm not aware of the report because I was appointed somewhere between the 15th and the 18th, but I never received a copy of a report of such a commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, are you able to state whether or not this is your signature or whether or not this is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a graphologist, but this doesn't look like my signature; however, the order could be an authentic one because I know that a commission did exist, and I recognise the names of all the individuals who were appointed as members of this commission. They are all local persons from the Konjic area, and this report does look authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember whether or not you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember signing it, but I do recall that a commission did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this could be your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be my signature. It looks like my signature, but it's not as well written out as I usually make it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you would agree with me that the interrogations of the prisoners were attended to, among other things, determine who was to be considered a prisoner of war and who was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That should be the role of the commission, that should have been -- but not about war or non-war, but it's more the degree of responsibility or guilt because, in most cases, these were people who were caught carrying weapons. Otherwise, they wouldn't have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree with me that the detainees were protected under the third Geneva Convention for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's a legal question. How can he answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask another question. Sir, you would agree that the Bosnian army considered that these persons were protected under the third Geneva Convention for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Explain to him "the third."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this witness already knows, but if he tells me he doesn't know, I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him if he knows about the third.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the third convention provides exactly, but I'm sure that these persons were protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask that this document be shown to you. It's a document given to us by the Delalic Defence. I have extra copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 238.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, whose signature is on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask my friend to wait until we have received the copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This should be my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say this should be your signature, does that mean it is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I truly do not recall seeing this document, but any expert could probably testify to it. But as far as the signature is concerned, yes, it does look like my signature, so probably it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that this document indicates that the detainees in the prison were protected under the third Geneva Convention for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is probably correct. If I probably signed it as a chief of staff, I had people who prepared such documents for me. And somebody probably knew precisely what the provisions of the third Geneva Conventions are and, at that time, I may have known that myself. I think it concerns human rights and protection of war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the last documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, these last documents refer to investigation commissions. Is it your testimony that even though you were involved in these documents, no one ever attempted to ascertain what happened to the investigation committee that had operated in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question? I got an incomplete interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, could you please repeat your answer, I believe there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was not the answer, you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's me, I'm sorry, I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, these last documents refer to the investigation commission that was being set up to interrogate the prisoners, is it your testimony that even though you were involved in this, the subsequent investigations, you never made any inquiry into what happened to the June, 1992, investigation commission? To find out what happened to them or their results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the 4th corps command, which would have been the appropriate authority were ordering me to tell me what I should do, it is not my job to question and inquire about the reasons. I have no reason to do that. In the last analysis, I had a commander and myself or Mr. Dragan Andric would often substitute for him, but we were not the ones who made any determination in this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect to the commission that was set up on January 5th, the document that you recognised, that indicates that the commission is to give a report, did you receive that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, again, let me tell you, the municipal headquarters was transformed again. It was actually changed because the Sirag (phoen) 7th brigade was established and then the 45th brigade was established and a number of people from municipal headquarters went to positions there. And in January, a new municipal headquarters was established with completely new personnel. Very, very few people were left from the old one. So there was no continuity with respect to what the old municipal staff was doing. And then immediately after that you have Gordnia Pacov (phoen) and the conflict between the HVO and the TO and then it went on until -- this way until 1994, when you had the final exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood your testimony, on January 5th of 1993, you signed an order appointing a commission and ordering the commission to give a report showing the following, who is was subject to court, who is not, et cetera, correct? You have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on these documents, yes, that is how it looks look like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on January 15th, some 10 days later, you, yourself, are appointed head of municipal headquarters, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, so my question is, did you receive the report from the commission that you appointed on the 5th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, the competence or the authority over the prison which I had while I was substituting for the commander was taken away from me, so the municipal headquarters was no -- had no longer any authority over the prison. The authority passed to the brigades. So I could not have received such a report any more. I was not -- and I was not a person who could have been in charge of that. Either of this commission, and I am referring now to the period when this new municipal headquarters was established. The authority over the prison was transferred to the brigades. It was not with the municipal headquarters any longer. So if this report was ever sent, it may have been sent to one of the brigades, not to the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, did I understand you that in January, the authority over prisons was, including Musala prison was taken away from municipal headquarters entirely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without Musala, that was the only prison where the -- where the prisoners were still being held and the municipal headquarters did not have any authority over the Musala prison after January.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they got into some new areas on cross-examination, and pursuant to the order of the court, I would like permission to explore these new areas. The order, I think, said that if we requested that, it would be fairly freely granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There aren't any new areas which are disclosed. Now cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he could start with this man's expertise as an international lawyer on the Geneva conventions. He actually testified, though, that there were certain people that had certain legal status’s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was talking about being in expressed by the command, if you read the order. It is ordered that in the proceedings, proceeded the provisions, it has been ordered to treat it as such. Not that he says it was his own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, he testified that certain persons had the status of prisoners of war. He directly testified to that -- .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is merely reproducing what is in the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They were so described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to argue with the court. Could I have five minutes of the court's time, it's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, unless it arose out of it, but I don't think it did because they were merely discussing the contents of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, prior to that, he was asked directly the status, there was commission to decide upon persons who were held in the camp and whether they were prisoners of war or civilians and he made the flat statement that they were prisoners of war and that is the area I would like to explore, not what the order says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They've been treated as such. Whether they were inside that prison or not is a question of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with the court wholeheartedly. I just wanted to make sure that that was clear, that he is not making that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He did not. If you look at it absolutely, it's there, clearly states it. Even the fact of the Geneva Convention, everything was stated there, and regarding them as war prisoners was stated there, not that he was volunteering that opinion. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think the person to answer that question was the General Kevric when he appeared in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I recall that testimony. I just didn't want this man's testimony to be given legal weight as opposed to factual weight. The court has obviously found my reservations, and the court's obviously found my reservations and I think that's all I need to do so thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be allowed, may I just say something in connection with this document? If you follow it carefully, I don't know how it has been translated, it says that we have been ordered, and that is the municipal staff, the command of the 4th corps has ordered us to act in accordance of the provisions of the third Geneva Conventions. None of us are experts of international law. It is the command that gives us orders to act in accordance with those provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What the court is saying, it was not your opinion that you are obeying this Geneva Convention or not. It was the order which states what you should do. Now, Ms. Residovic, what is your re-examination, if there's any, in respect of areas that have arisen from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will have some brief questions, but before that, before addressing the witness, the last documents tendered by my learned friend, Ms. McHenry into evidence, according to my translation, I heard that it was the last orders shown to you, so I don't know whether you're referring to the order of 5th January, 1993. If that order is included, I just wish to note that this order has already been admitted into evidence through the witness Bektacovic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was given number 238, and its own requests, it's date 29th December, 1992. It's quite different from that of the 5th of January, if you notice it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because I have been given another document of the 29th of December, '92 and as it wasn't quite precise, and to be able to keep track of the evidence, could my learned friend check whether these are the documents we are referring to? I am doing my best to follow, but I feel there is a little confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you think it's fair? If you have areas in issue, pursue that, and if there's any ambiguity, we will clarify that. If you have any re-examination arising out of the cross-examination, if you have none, we know this witness is concluded, his testimony, and then we'll decide what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will have some re-examination related to the cross-examination by the Prosecutor. Re-examination by Ms. Residovic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, you said that at one point in time in July 1992, you took over command over a unit in the area Tisavica. Will you tell me, please, under whose order did you take over command of a combat unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By orders of the commander Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the cross-examination, you also said that towards the end of June, Mr. Delalic became a member of the TO and went to Vranske Stijene. My question is: In executing this task, did Mr. Delalic have any command military function or was it the function of an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the function of an ordinary soldier and I think that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic, you said that that was the first time, and that is a month before he became commander, that was the first time that Mr. Delalic became a member of the Territorial Defence. Tell me, from April until he went into the Oganj Operation, was Mr. Delalic a civilian or a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tahirovic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you're discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address the court with a request, please? Just one minute, a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any good reasons for doing so, because you're no longer a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it need not be as a witness, it is not directly related, but it is related to my testimony here last time. At one of the satellite programs, there is a daily Hague report, and the picture is probably broadcast from here. Asked by Ms. Residovic whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic was ever a commander of the Territorial Defence, my answer is no, and actually what is shown is a recording which should disprove what I said. Afterwards, that tape was shown on Belgrade Television. I think that, in a sense, this is extremely incorrect with relation to me and my personal integrity and the position that I took here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Was part of your evidence before the Tribunal also recorded and shown, part of your evidence before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just when Ms. Risedovic asked me whether Zejnil Delalic was ever a TO commander, and my answer is no. And after that, a recording is shown which should prove that I am lying. I think that this is not fair and I think we should pay attention in the future because these are programs watched by the whole world and I consider it insulting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Recordings are authenticated, and I am sure your counsel knows about the recording. If it's inaccurate, I am sure they would have objected to it. In any event, I suppose we have heard you. I'm not aware of any such confusion. Thank you very much for your assistance. I am grateful for pointing out, perhaps, any such error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, linked to the remark made by the witness, the Defence has heard from many quarters that this part of the proceedings is being incorrectly reported, and I wish to inform you that we will address the registry of the Tribunal and ask to see these recordings and request that this Tribunal insist on objective reporting on what this Tribunal is doing. I didn't consider it necessary for me to speak because I was not aware of what the witness was going to say, but I do wish to inform you that the Defence counsel will address the registry which is responsible for objective reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have already mentioned it to him and I mentioned what could be done. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any other witness, let's have him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence calls witness Midhat Cerovac. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for complying with the order of the trial chamber, but I still observe a lot of duplication of your witnesses and far more than that. I don't know what you're doing by that type of approach. It's a very difficult thing for one to hear the same thing four, five, six times. As I said last time during our status conference, I don't think a number of times for which a thing is said makes any difference to its voracity or its acceptability by the Trial Chamber, but you might still discuss further at the status conference what is besetting the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask this witness to show the role and responsibility of a coordinator and TG-1 commander, and you also were examining Hadzihuseinovic in this regard. Why don't you pick one of them on the same subject? In fact, I think Hadzihuseinovic probably would be in a better position to tell us. He was the president of the war presidency. What precisely was the role assigned to him as a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The number of witnesses isn't what proves the point. It's the quality of the evidence that is important. One witness may be sufficient if his evidence is really reliable, but you're examining at least two witnesses, one and two, on the same subject. Maybe you can keep those questions for Hadzihuseinovic who was the president of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For those reasons, we called the witness Hadzihuseinovic, but you are well aware of the charges against my client, and the Prosecutor has not changed those charges to this moment. I also do not think that the number of witnesses may prove a fact to be true or not, but so far during the testimony of the prosecution witnesses, we have only heard and seen witnesses who have indirectly spoken about the situation in Konjic and the functions of my client. You drew our attention, during the expert witness testimony, that some documents may only corroborate an opinion, but that those witnesses cannot authenticate a document because they were not familiar with them at the time, nor can they be fact witnesses. Now, in order to give the Trial Chamber an opportunity to make a fair judgement, but also for the Trial Chamber to really learn about what happened there, even though it may have been very complicated in conditions of war, we're calling eyewitnesses who were on the spot, who held certain positions. We will call people, the chief of staff of the tactical group and first commander of the tactical group, if necessary, because we want you to know what happened there. It is not the same when you hear things from somebody who was never there or who came there after the events or, rather, someone who was a direct participate in those events. And that is for those reasons that we feel it may be for you to hear even three times that people didn't have enough to eat, because we have heard at least 50 times that people only got one slice of bread. I don't say that the number of repetitions is important, but an assessment of what the previous witness said will probably depend on what you hear from this witness. Maybe ten witnesses are sufficient to cover all areas, but if we bring 20 who will complement one another because each one of them does not have the same duties. Because I still remember the suggestion of the president that the court has to establish the truth, and I know that a criminal court has to see whether the prosecution has proven the charges or not. But when a court has to assess what happened in Konjic and why it happened, I think that the facts are also important. The moment when you tell us that this fact has been cleared up from the standpoint of the Trial Chamber or if the prosecution quashes account, we would no longer need to call so many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we understand you. I indicated during the course of the week we're likely to have a status conference to, perhaps, flesh out some of these difficulties. We might as well carry on with this witness until such a time as a proper action has been taken. Let's swear him and carry on with the evidence that you are presenting. Thank you. Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat. MIDHAT CEROVAC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, will you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber by telling us your first and last names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Midhat Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, before I continue with the examination, it is my duty, for your own benefit and the benefit of the Trial Chamber, to warn you that we speak the same language, so we may tend to speak very quickly, but we need to make ourselves understood in this courtroom. So, please, when I put a question to you, please listen to hear the end of the translation on the headphones on the table. When you hear that the translation is over, only then answer the question because, in that way, all your answers will completely be translated. Please, turn up the volume on the headphones, and when you hear the end of my translation, answer my question. I apologise for wasting time on such technical matters, but I think it is important. Mr. Cerovac, will you please tell the Trial Chamber when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 18th of October, 1940 and I'm a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- 1960, sorry and I'm a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what is your educational background and your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed primary and secondary school in Konjic and my studies in Sarajevo in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you and what were you doing in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1992, I was working as a head of security and intelligence in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, could you tell the court what were your duties in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, I had the following duties: I said that when the war started, my position was in the municipal staff as head of security and intelligence matters. When the war broke out, I was an operations officer in the municipal staff. I was chief of staff of the municipal staff. I was an officer for operations and training in the joint command of the TO and the HVO, and I was also assistant chief of staff for operations and training and assistant chief of staff in the joint command. At the end of 1992, I took over the post of brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When were you demobilised from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was demobilised in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, were you wounded during the war and do you have certain traumatic consequences from the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was wounded in 1994. I was very seriously wounded in the immediate vicinity of the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of those traumatic experiences, you can speak frankly before this Tribunal about the facts you are familiar with; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I shall do my best to convey to the court all facts so that it may establish the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have been told by the interpreters to ask you to slow down a little bit, and so please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of those duties that you performed in the course of 1992, could you tell us what was happening in the territorial defence in Konjic in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In what respect? In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please specify which field you have in mind when you are talking about changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about changes in the reorganisation of the Territorial Defence and its transformation into the army. I think the witness understands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand my question? Do you know what was happening? As a member of the staff in April 1992, did any changes occur in the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. According to our chain of command structure, we were subordinated to the district TO staff, and then the vertical chain of command and control went towards the republican staff of the TO based in Sarajevo. Sometime in the first half of April, the presidency of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a decree on Territorial Defence making certain corrections in the sense that the republican TO staff was being abolished. And republican staff of Territory Defence was being formed so that all the municipal and district staffs in the system of control and command have to be subordinated to, as I just said, the newly formed republican staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, did the municipal TO staff organise itself in accordance with these instructions coming from the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the court when this happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said "middle of April." The middle of April, he has already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The witness said when the regulations were passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But my question is whether they acted in Konjic in accordance with those regulations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We did act in accordance with those regulations because we had to respect the decisions of our presidency. I know that at a meeting of the municipal assembly of Konjic, a proposal was made for the new commander of the municipal TO staff and the municipal assembly proposed as the new commander, Mr. Enver Redzepovic. He is a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who abandoned, who deserted, from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, Mr. Mucic begs to be excused for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may be excused for a few minutes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, in accordance with those provisional instructions, was the municipal staff subordinated to the district staff in Mostar and, if that did not happen, who was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
